title: Basic Tomato Gravy
author: Fran Osseo-Asare
desc: Eight tomatoes, a large onion and a quarter cup of oil — the plain gravy that other dishes are measured against by the cupful.
longDesc: This is the plainest sauce in the Ghanaian repertoire and it exists to be measured into other things. Eight tomatoes, which come to about two cups with their juice, a large onion, a quarter cup of oil, half to one teaspoon of salt, and a few tablespoons of tomato paste if you want it. It is the gravy that ayikple calls for by volume — a cup and a third to a cup and a half — and it is the thing a Ghanaian kitchen keeps in a bowl to spoon over rice, beans or boiled yam without further thought.
steps: Chop or blend the tomatoes to about 2 cups with their juice.
Heat the oil and soften the onion.
Add the tomatoes and the optional tomato paste.
Cook down until the gravy thickens and the oil comes back to the surface.
Use at once, or keep for spooning over rice, beans or yam.
chefTips: Eight tomatoes to about two cups with juice is the useful conversion here, and it tells you to keep the juice rather than draining it.
A quarter cup of oil for six servings is modest. The oil coming back to the surface is the standard signal that a West African tomato base is cooked.
The tomato paste is optional and it is there for colour and depth rather than volume. A few tablespoons is the printed amount.
Salt range of half to one teaspoon — start low, since this gravy usually ends up in something else that is already seasoned.
Make it to go into ayikple, which calls for a cup and a third to a cup and a half by volume. That is roughly a batch and a half of this recipe's yield, so scale up if that is the plan.
No cooking time or doneness cue is printed in the source. The twenty-five minutes above and the oil cue are both editorial.
Keep a bowl in the fridge. This is the Ghanaian equivalent of a basic tomato sauce and it makes a plate of plain rice into a meal.
commonMistakes: A full teaspoon of salt when it is going into a seasoned dish.
Not cooking it long enough for the oil to separate.
Treating the tomato paste as essential.
Scaling it one-for-one for ayikple, which needs more.
sources: Adapted from 'Recipe #63: Basic tomato gravy and #64 Ayikple', betumiblog.blogspot.com. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Posted by Fran at 3:47 PM', timestamped 2011-06-25. ALL QUANTITIES SINGLE-PASS AND UNVERIFIED — the page was read once only.
Ingredients exactly as printed: ¼ cup oil; 8 tomatoes (about 2 cups with juice); a few tablespoons of paste (optional); 1 large onion; ½-1 teaspoon salt. That is the complete list.

NO METHOD STEPS, NO COOKING TIME AND NO DONENESS CUE are printed for this gravy. The method above is the standard sequence for a West African tomato base — soften the onion in the oil, add the tomato and paste, cook down until the oil surfaces — and it is labelled as editorial rather than quoted. The 25-minute cook time is likewise an estimate.
NO YIELD is printed. The six servings above is an editorial reading of eight tomatoes.

ITS ROLE AS A MEASURED COMPONENT: ayikple, published from the same post at GHA046, calls for '1⅓–1½ cups tomato gravy' by volume, which is what makes this a defined preparation rather than a generic sauce.
THE OIL IS UNSPECIFIED as to type, unlike most Ghanaian recipes which name palm oil or vegetable oil. It is reproduced as printed.

WHY IT IS PUBLISHED DESPITE BEING THIN: it is the only Ghanaian basic tomato gravy quantified anywhere in the material consulted, and another published recipe depends on it by volume. Publishing it with its gaps named is more useful than leaving a dangling reference.
healthBenefits: Cooked tomato is high in lycopene, more bioavailable with the oil present.
A good source of vitamin C and potassium.
Modest oil content for a West African base.
culturalNote: Every cuisine has its default tomato sauce and this is Ghana's — unremarkable on its own, and the reason a plate of rice, a boiled yam or a pot of beans is never dry. That it was written down at all, and quantified well enough for another recipe to measure it by the cup, is more than most household basics get.
